lines: Most days this line's energy total looks exactly like every other day.
Then one day it comes back astronomical, after a meter got swapped out for a new one.
A fix applied the week before, meant to clean up a different problem, had already quietly thrown away a real event without anyone noticing.
Here's the one habit worth locking in before anything else.
A meter's own reading never resets itself on its own. It only ever climbs.
So how much was used in a given stretch of time is always a subtraction of two readings. That subtraction is reliable right up until the register itself does something unusual.
Worth reasoning through before the next few reveals answer it directly.
Subtract an earlier reading from a later one and the result comes back negative.
Does that one fact alone tell you what actually happened to the meter?
answer: It doesn't, and that's the whole trap.
A negative result can come from at least three completely different events, and each one needs its own, different repair.
Treating all three the same way is how a fix for one quietly breaks the other two.

lines: Take the case where the register simply runs out of digits and wraps back around.
That sounds like lost information, but it genuinely isn't.
Once you know exactly how wide that register is, the true amount used across the wrap comes back out exactly, with nothing left to guess at.
Now the harder case: the device itself restarts, and its counter falls back down near nothing.
Whatever was used between the last good reading and that restart is simply gone from the record.
There's no clever formula that pulls that number back out of thin air. The honest thing to produce is a ceiling, built from how much time passed and the fastest this line is ever known to run.
Compare that honest ceiling against what used to happen here.
The older approach just threw out any negative result and quietly recorded zero for that stretch.
That's not a smaller version of the right answer. It's a confident, wrong one, standing in for an honest range nobody bothered to compute.
A third case looks nothing like the first two.
The physical equipment stays exactly where it is, but a brand new meter goes in, starting its own count from its own fresh zero.
Subtract straight across that boundary and you get a huge, meaningless number. Treat each side of the boundary as its own separate story, and the real figures on both sides fall right out.
Switch from counting to a different kind of reading entirely: a rate, sampled at whatever moments happened to be convenient.
Properly accounting for how far apart those moments actually were gives one number.
Pretending they were evenly spaced, and just averaging them, gives a different number that looks just as plausible on a page.
One shared meter sits upstream of several lines at once, and somebody has to decide how much of its total belongs to any one of them.
Split it by how many hours each line actually ran, and you get one answer.
Split the exact same total by how many parts each line actually made, and you get a different one.
That gap between them isn't noise. Turn it into a price, and it's a number someone in a budget meeting would actually argue about.
A subtraction that breaks three separate ways, each with its own distinct fix.
A loss that gets bounded honestly rather than papered over with a zero.
A boundary that gets split instead of subtracted straight across.
A rate handled as the varying thing it actually is, not flattened into a single average.
And a split-the-difference decision that turns directly into real money, once you bother to price it.
Someone needs exactly one figure for how much energy went into each good part, for a line fed by that same shared upstream meter.
Does which splitting rule got used actually change the number that ends up in the report?
answer: The energy that meter actually used is a fixed fact once it's measured.
How much of that fact gets assigned to any one line was always a choice, and the final figure simply carries that choice along with it.
